records.name: Pasco
records.current_summary:
Pasco has no documented trans-specific regional law, ordinance or enforcement pattern; the binding framework is national. In February 2025 the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved the dictamen of bills 6506 and 8457, barring trans people from public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than their birth sex — narrow exceptions for custody, medical care and accompanying children under 12, the elderly or disabled — and prohibiting ambiguous signage. On 2 April 2025 the plenary approved the fused text without a second vote; a national human-rights institute's legal analysis reads Article 5.1 as violating constitutional equality and inter-American non-discrimination standards. The trigger was a July 2023 complaint about gendered restroom labels at the capital's international airport, and activists note enforcement would rest on individual security staff judging IDs.

No Pasco-specific findings exist to move it off the national position.

sources.claim: Infobae Peru (20 Feb 2025): the congressional Comision de Mujer y Familia approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457 (sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante) that would prohibit any person from entering public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to their birth sex, with narrow exceptions (custody, and cases where required, including accompanying minors, the elderly or people with disabilities), and would oblige venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs; the article notes the text still needed plenary backing and reports the trigger as the July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport. Activist Gianna Camacho is quoted arguing the measure is discriminatory and that enforcement would rest on security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender. This is the national framework this department is scored against; the article contains no Pasco-specific content.

IDEHPUCP legal analysis (15 April 2025, Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte): on Wednesday 2 April 2025 the plenary of Congress approved and waived a second vote on the dictamen of the 'Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los ninos y adolescentes', whose Article 5.1 prohibits persons from entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than their birth sex. The institute reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination (Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights), resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors, and recalls documented cases of trans people barred from public restrooms - including SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022 dismissing a trans woman's discrimination complaint against SmartFit, where the company grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the DNI - and the fact that gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive. This is the national framework this department is scored against; the article contains no Pasco-specific content.

records.name: El Callao
records.current_summary: No region-specific trans law, ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding was located for this division - the research dossier lists it among the units with no sub-national signal, so the national evidence applies: the congressional Women and Family Committee approved bills banning trans people from public restrooms in early 2025 (floor vote pending), and the national university observatory recorded 54 LGBTI homicides and 170 rights violations in 2020-2023, more than half of the homicide victims trans women (30 of 54). The absence of local findings reflects Peru's lack of hate-crime statistics rather than any positive local difference.

records.name: Ucayali
records.current_summary:
The documented evidence binding a trans visitor in Ucayali is national in scope. In February 2025 the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved bills 6506 and 8457 barring trans people from public restrooms corresponding to their gender rather than their birth sex, with narrow exceptions for custody, medical care and accompanying children under 12, the elderly or disabled, and a ban on ambiguous signage; the plenary approved the fused law on 2 April 2025 without a second vote, in a package a national human-rights institute frames as legalized discrimination against trans access to public space. A July 2023 complaint over gendered bathroom labels at the capital's airport set the process in motion; activists object that the measures weaponize stigma.

Ucayali has no recorded local ordinance, incident series or enforcement pattern, and official data carry no departmental breakdown — the national framework is the only documented determinant of conditions here.

sources.claim: Infobae Perú (20 Feb 2025) reports the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a draft opinion (dictamen) merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex, with exceptions for custody, where medical attention is required, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, plus a ban on 'ambiguous' bathroom signage; the trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over the Jorge Chávez airport's gendered restroom labels. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho calls the measure discriminatory, warning that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment (including ID checks), and notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. It contains no Ucayali-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding; for this record its value is the national ban on gender-matching restroom access that binds the region (committee stage, February 2025).

IDEHPUCP legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte (15 Apr 2025) confirms that on Wednesday 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved and exempted from second vote a bill whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', save for narrow listed exceptions, and argues this directly violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The authors say the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype implicitly presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. It contains no Ucayali-specific finding; for this record its value is the human-rights institute's analysis of the national framework that governs the region.
